claims.text: Calling toString on an Output<T> in Pulumi produces placeholder text of the form `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`.
A page exists at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ titled 'Output value errors' that describes this and other symptoms of treating an output as if it were already a plain value.
The placeholder text `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported` can appear in a log line, a generated file, or a resource property when an Output is treated as a plain value.
The page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ exists and covers diagnosing errors from stringifying, branching on, or reading a Pulumi output value like a plain value.
Pulumi Cloud returns a "409 conflict: Another update is currently in progress" error when an update is already in progress.
The page /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/update-conflicts/ exists.
Pulumi Cloud can return 500 internal server errors.
When the Pulumi CLI can't access a self-managed (DIY) state backend, it produces a `read ".pulumi/meta.yaml"` error; the DIY backend page has an anchor #error-reading-pulumimetayaml.
On Apple Silicon Macs, x86_64 binaries running under Rosetta 2 can cause crashes or hangs in Pulumi.
A recently deleted stack can be recovered from the Pulumi Cloud console, including after an accidental `pulumi stack rm --force`.
Pulumi supports `--target` and `--exclude` flags to limit operations to specific resources.
Pulumi offers automatic logging, CLI verbose logging, and program logging for debugging.
Pulumi dev builds are pre-release builds that provide bug fixes that haven't shipped in a stable release yet.
Running `pulumi logs share` securely sends the logs from a failed operation to the Pulumi team.
The logging guide at /docs/iac/operations/debugging/logging/ has an 'automatic-logging' anchor covering `pulumi logs share`.
`pulumi destroy` can fail in some scenarios, which the destroy-failures page addresses.
Pulumi has a Community Slack at slack.pulumi.com offering community support.
Pulumi offers paid support options.
Pulumi resource properties are represented as Outputs rather than plain values because their real values are not known until the resource providing them has been created or updated.
Outputs being unknown until resource creation is central to how Pulumi builds a dependency graph and runs `pulumi preview`.

When an output value is concatenated, logged, or converted to a string directly instead of via `apply` or an equivalent helper, Pulumi does not raise an error by default but silently substitutes a placeholder message for the value.
In TypeScript, converting an Output to a string yields literal text such as `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`, followed by guidance to use `apply` or `pulumi.interpolate`.
In TypeScript, calling `JSON.stringify()` on an output, or letting one flow into a JSON body, produces a `Calling [toJSON] on an [Output<T>] is not supported` string rather than the value.

In Python, using an Output in an f-string produces a broken string containing text such as `Calling __str__ on an Output[T] is not supported`, and Pulumi also logs a warning without raising an exception.
In Python, passing an Output to `json.dumps()` fails with `TypeError: Object of type Output is not JSON serializable`.
In Python, `Output.json_dumps()` is the way to serialize an output to JSON.
In Go, passing a `pulumi.StringOutput` where a `string` is expected is a compile error.
In Go, output values are resolved with `ApplyT`.
In C#, converting an Output to a string yields literal text such as `Calling [ToString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`, followed by guidance to use `Apply` or `Output.Format`.
Setting the environment variable `PULUMI_ERROR_OUTPUT_STRING=true` makes string conversion of an output throw an exception instead of returning placeholder text, in TypeScript, Python, and C#.

Because the placeholder mistake does not throw, the program runs and `pulumi up` succeeds, with the placeholder text surfacing later in logs, generated config files, or downstream resource properties.

String-composition helpers for outputs are `pulumi.interpolate` and `pulumi.concat` in TypeScript, `Output.concat`/`Output.format`/`Output.json_dumps` in Python, `pulumi.Sprintf`/`pulumi.JSONMarshal` in Go, and `Output.Format` in C#.

A value read from an output inside an `apply` callback and assigned to an outer variable is not available outside the callback; the callback runs asynchronously after the output resolves, generally after top-level program code has finished, so the outer variable is still undefined.
Adding a delay cannot fix the apply-callback timing issue because the callback runs when the engine resolves the dependency graph, not on the program's clock.
An Output such as `bucket.bucketName` can be passed directly as an input to another resource (e.g. `aws.s3.BucketObject`'s `bucket` property) without apply.
Most resource inputs accept outputs as well as plain values, though a handful of positions such as a resource's logical name cannot.
In a dynamically typed language, an `if` on an output evaluates the output object rather than its eventual value and is generally always true.
In a statically typed language, branching on an `Output<bool>` is usually a compile error because an `Output<bool>` is not a `bool`.

A value known when the program starts, such as a stack configuration setting read with `pulumi.Config`, an environment variable, or a hardcoded flag, is a plain value that can be branched on normally.
In TypeScript, `vpc.vpcId.apply((id) => ...)` derives a new Output whose value depends on the branch.
Passing an output as a resource's logical name, loop bound, or map key fails to compile in TypeScript, Go, and C#, where these positions are typed as plain strings or numbers.
In Python, passing an output as a resource's logical name raises `TypeError: Expected resource name to be a string`.
In Python, using an output as a loop bound (`range(some_output)`) raises `TypeError: 'Output' object cannot be interpreted as an integer`.
In Python, using an output as a dictionary key does not raise; Python compares and hashes the output object itself, so the lookup silently keys on the wrong thing.

When resource names or counts depend on data only known after a resource is created, one fix is to provision dependent resources in a later, separate stack that consumes the first stack's outputs through a StackReference.

Pulumi has no supported way to block the program and pull a resolved value out of an output synchronously; awaiting or reading an output synchronously either doesn't compile, fails at runtime, or returns placeholder text.
Synchronous unwrapping of outputs is disallowed deliberately because the engine would need the value before it has determined the order in which to create resources.
`pulumi stack output <name>` reads a single stack output from the CLI after a deployment.
A StackReference lets one Pulumi program consume another stack's outputs as inputs.
The Automation API exposes an `outputs` field on the result of running an update (e.g. `res.Outputs` in Go).

Linked pages exist: /docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/, /docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/apply/, /docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/all/, /docs/iac/concepts/stacks/#stackreferences, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
